## Untyped $\lambda$-calculus

### Exercise 1.1

Write $M[x:=N,y:=L]$ for the *simultaneous* substitution: every free $x$ and every free $y$ in $M$ is replaced at the same time, by $N$ and by $L$ respectively. On the right below stands the sequential substitution of the lecture, one variable after the other.
$$
    M[x:=N,y:=L] \equiv M[x:=N][y:=L]
$$

Show that this is not always true, and state a condition on $y$ and $N$ under which the two sides do agree.<br>
<span style="font-size: 80%;">Nederpelt & Geuvers, <em>Type Theory and Formal Proof</em> (CUP, 2014), Exercise 1.6.</span>


::: {.callout-note title="Definitions" icon="false"}

**Substitution** (Def. 1.6.1). With $\equiv$ syntactic identity,
$$
\begin{aligned}
x[x := N] &\equiv N,
& y[x := N] &\equiv y \quad (y \neq x), \\[8pt]
(PQ)[x := N] &\equiv (P[x := N])(Q[x := N]), & (\lambda y.P)[x := N] &\equiv
\lambda z.P^{y \to z}[x := N].
\end{aligned}
$$
where in the last clause $\lambda z.P^{y \to z}$ is an $\alpha$-variant of $\lambda y.P$ with $z \notin \operatorname{FV}(N)$, and $P^{y \to z}$ is $P$ with every free $y$ renamed to $z$.

**Free variables** (Def. 1.4.1). $\operatorname{FV}(x) = \{x\}, \operatorname{FV}(PQ) = \operatorname{FV}(P) \cup \operatorname{FV}(Q), \operatorname{FV}(\lambda x.P) = \operatorname{FV}(P) \setminus \{x\}$.

:::

**Answer.** Let $M=x, N=y, L=z$. Then:

- simultaneous substitution: $M[x:=N,y:=L] = x[x:=y,y:=z] = y$.
- sequential substitution: $M[x:=N][y:=L] = x[x:=y][y:=z] = y[y:=z] = z$.

The two sides agree if $y \notin \operatorname{FV}(N)$, i.e., if $y$ does not occur free in $N$.

### Exercise 1.2

The first three *Church numerals*, and two terms mimicking addition and multiplication on them, are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathit{zero} &:= \lambda f x.\, x,
& \mathit{one} &:= \lambda f x.\, f\, x,
& \mathit{two} &:= \lambda f x.\, f\,(f\,x), \\
\mathit{add} &:= \lambda m n f x.\, m\, f\, (n\, f\, x),
& \mathit{mult} &:= \lambda m n f x.\, m\,(n\, f)\,x.
\end{aligned}
$$

(a) Show that $\mathit{add}\ \mathit{one}\ \mathit{one} \twoheadrightarrow_\beta \mathit{two}$.
(b) Prove that $\mathit{add}\ \mathit{one}\ \mathit{one} \neq_\beta \mathit{mult}\ \mathit{one}\ \mathit{zero}$.

<span style="color: gray; font-size: 85%;">Nederpelt & Geuvers, *Type Theory and Formal Proof* (CUP, 2014), Exercise 1.10.</span>

::: {.callout-note .definitions-box title="Definitions" icon="false"}

**Reduction** (Defs. 1.8.1, 1.8.3, 1.8.5). One step is $(\lambda x.M)N \to_\beta M[x:=N]$, applied anywhere inside a term; $M \twoheadrightarrow_\beta N$ is a chain of zero or more such steps, and $M =_\beta N$ is a chain in which each step may go either way.

**Normal form** (Def. 1.9.1). $M$ is in $\beta$-normal form if it contains no redex $(\lambda x.P)Q$.

**Church–Rosser** (Thm. 1.9.8). If $M \twoheadrightarrow_\beta N$ and $M \twoheadrightarrow_\beta L$, then $N \twoheadrightarrow_\beta R$ and $L \twoheadrightarrow_\beta R$ for some $R$. Hence a term has at most one $\beta$-normal form (Lem. 1.9.10(2)).

:::

**Answer.**

(a) We show that $\mathit{add}\ \mathit{one}\ \mathit{one} \twoheadrightarrow_\beta \mathit{two}$ by successive $\beta$-reductions.
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathit{add}\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{one} \\[6pt]
&= (\lambda m n f x.\, m\,f\,(n\,f\,x))\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{one} \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta (\lambda n f x.\, \mathit{one}\,f\,(n\,f\,x))\,\mathit{one} \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta \lambda f x.\, \mathit{one}\,f\,(\mathit{one}\,f\,x) \\[6pt]
&= \lambda f x.\, (\lambda g y.\, g\,y)\,f\,(\mathit{one}\,f\,x) \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta \lambda f x.\, (\lambda y.\, f\,y)\,(\mathit{one}\,f\,x) \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta \lambda f x.\, f\,(\mathit{one}\,f\,x) \\[6pt]
&= \lambda f x.\, f\,((\lambda g y.\,g\,y)\,f\,x) \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta \lambda f x.\, f\,((\lambda y.\,f\,y)\,x) \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta \lambda f x.\, f\,(f\,x) \\[6pt]
&= \mathit{two}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence,
$$
\boxed{
\mathit{add}\ \mathit{one}\ \mathit{one}
\twoheadrightarrow_\beta \mathit{two}.
}
$$


(b) We prove that
$$
\mathit{add}\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{one}
\neq_\beta
\mathit{mult}\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{zero}.
$$

First, by part (a),
$$
\mathit{add}\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{one}
\twoheadrightarrow_\beta
\mathit{two}
=
\lambda f x.\,f\,(f\,x).
$$

Observe that $\mathit{two}$ is in $\beta$-normal form, since it contains no $\beta$-redex of the form $(\lambda x.\,P)\,Q$.

Next, consider $\mathit{mult}\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{zero}$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathit{mult}\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{zero} \\[6pt]
&= (\lambda m n f x.\,m\,(n\,f)\,x)\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{zero} \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta (\lambda n f x.\,\mathit{one}\,(n\,f)\,x)\,\mathit{zero} \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta \lambda f x.\,\mathit{one}\,(\mathit{zero}\,f)\,x \\[6pt]
&= \lambda f x.\,(\lambda g y.\,g\,y)\,((\lambda u v.\,v)\,f)\,x \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta \lambda f x.\,(\lambda g y.\,g\,y)\,(\lambda v.\,v)\,x \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta \lambda f x.\,(\lambda y.\,(\lambda v.\,v)\,y)\,x \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta \lambda f x.\,(\lambda v.\,v)\,x \\[6pt]
&\to_\beta \lambda f x.\,x \\[6pt]
&= \mathit{zero}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,
$$
\mathit{mult}\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{zero}
\twoheadrightarrow_\beta \mathit{zero}.
$$

Moreover, $\mathit{zero}=\lambda f x.\,x$ is also in $\beta$-normal form.

Suppose, for contradiction, that
$$
\mathit{add}\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{one}
=_\beta
\mathit{mult}\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{zero}.
$$

By the **Church–Rosser theorem**, $\beta$-equivalent terms must have the same $\beta$-normal form (up to $\alpha$-equivalence).

However,
$$
\mathit{two}=\lambda f x.\,f\,(f\,x)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathit{zero}=\lambda f x.\,x
$$
are distinct $\beta$-normal forms and are not $\alpha$-equivalent.

This is a contradiction. Therefore,
$$
\boxed{
\mathit{add}\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{one}
\neq_\beta
\mathit{mult}\,\mathit{one}\,\mathit{zero}.
}
$$
